title: These 'Sovereign Citizens' Don't Believe They're Part of the US
summary: News interview on sovereign citizens' 1871-corporation belief, far-right roots and QAnon adopting their March 4 inauguration claim.

assertions.quote: spinning out from radical right-wing movements in the 1970s

verdicts.note: A footnote says US OPCA ideas incubated in right-wing Militia, Aryan Nations and Christian Identity communities and grew in the 1980s farm debt crisis; Posse Comitatus is not named and Canada had a separate tax-protest lineage.
This law review traces the 1990s movement to four overlapping groups: Posse Comitatus, Patriot/militia groups, common-law courts and anti-tax protestors.
The review, citing Loeser, traces the movement's origins to the Posse Comitatus, tax protestors and militias.

assertions.quote: the idea that the united states stopped being a country and started being a corporation in 1871

verdicts.note: The Supreme Court describes the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia 'a body corporate for municipal purposes', a mere municipal corporation; sovereign power over the District stays with the US government and Congress.

assertions.quote: we've seen q1 followers starting to adopt sovereign citizen style arguments

verdicts.note: News reports in early 2021 documented QAnon channels promoting the 1871-based March 4 inauguration claim.

assertions.quote: it is certainly uh rooted deeply in conspiratorial thinking white nationalism and anti-semitism

verdicts.note: Its Posse Comitatus origins were racist and antisemitic, but today's movement includes many adherents, such as Moorish groups, without those beliefs.
The fractional-reserve theme traces to a Christian Identity pamphlet, but a sociological profile found the Canadian Freeman population predominantly left-leaning and ideologically heterogeneous.

Several gurus were anti-Semites or white supremacists and US roots lie in Aryan Nations, but the Canadian Freeman movement arose from leftist, green and anti-globalization circles and Detaxers were driven by greed.
The Posse Comitatus root held white-supremacist and Jewish-conspiracy beliefs, but the review says the movement was born only 'in part' out of right-wing extremism and has three other roots.
The START authors note that sovereigns do not share Klan-style supremacist views and focus on government abuse rather than minorities or Jews; this speaks to current focus more than historical roots.
Review says ideology overlaps with far-right and white-supremacy groups but also that the biggest recent growth has been among African Americans (Moorish sovereigns).
